doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Deciding on a career: album credits and liner notes
summary: As a child he read liner notes and credits, wanted to see his name on drums, and was fascinated by how records were made; Rowe did the same with saxophonists.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was there a point, I’m often curious with professional musicians who’ve had significant success if there was a point when you were young that you made a conscious decision to go into the field? Or did it just like sort of happen?

No. It’s what I wanted to do from an early age. I mean as soon as I could read I was reading the backs of the albums or reading the labels on the 78s that my father had. And I was just fascinated, you know, usually somebody’s liner notes, Orrin Keepnews or George Avakian or Nat Hentoff or someone you know and I would read the whole thing beginning to end and then read about the session if they had session details and then look at the credits. Oh my God Tony Williams on drums, Jo Jones on drums or whoever the drummer was. Elvin Jones on drums. And I just wanted to see my name on drums. That was — but not only the ego part of it but the process. I wanted to be in the studio and under the microphones, you know behind the microphones. And it was fascinating to me how records were made and how they did sessions and I imagined hours of rehearsal and the guys reading music and they have one take, two takes, three takes, how long did it take to get this performance that is documented here on this vinyl? The whole process was fascinating to me and I wanted to be involved in it as soon as I could.

It’s interesting you say that because I used to do the same thing. I was more attuned to the saxophone players so you’d see Jerome Richardson’s on this one, and now I notice he’s on that one and all these people like playing musical chairs and said, wow, I want to do that.
